label: Scaly plaques and patches
lead: The papulosquamous group is where most diagnostic errors in general dermatology are made, because psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, tinea and nummular eczema all produce red scaly plaques. Scrape before you commit — tinea incognito exists because that step was skipped.

stop.l: Erythroderma — confluent erythema over >90% of body surface
stop.a: Exfoliative erythroderma. Admit. Thermoregulatory failure, high-output cardiac failure, fluid and protein loss, and sepsis are the killers, not the rash. Establish the underlying cause: psoriasis, drug, atopic dermatitis, PRP, or cutaneous T cell lymphoma.

stop.l: Generalized pustules on erythema with fever and leukocytosis
stop.a: Generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) or AGEP. Admit. Stop any candidate drug started in the last 1–4 days. Fluids, and check calcium and albumin.

stop.l: Rapidly expanding scaly plaques with new lymphadenopathy in an older adult
stop.a: Consider erythrodermic mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome. Send flow cytometry for Sézary cells and a T cell receptor gene rearrangement study alongside biopsy.

stop.l: Sudden explosive psoriasis in a young adult with no family history
stop.a: Do HIV serology. Sudden-onset severe psoriasis is a recognized presenting feature of HIV infection.

stop.l: Scaly plaques with fever, arthritis and mucosal ulcers
stop.a: Consider reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum), acute lupus, or secondary syphilis. Serology before topical steroids.

stop.l: A solitary scaly plaque that persists or enlarges for months despite treatment
stop.a: Biopsy to exclude Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) or another cutaneous malignancy. A fixed, treatment-refractory solitary plaque is malignant until proven otherwise.

dx.n: Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
dx.look: A slowly enlarging, sharply demarcated, erythematous, slightly scaly or crusted plaque, most often on sun-exposed or lower-leg skin of an older adult; it persists and enlarges despite topical treatment and is regularly mistaken for psoriasis, eczema or a seborrheic keratosis.
fr: Solitary, fixed, sharply marginated plaque that slowly enlarges
Persists or grows despite adequate topical steroid or antifungal
Sun-exposed skin, lower legs of older women, or prior arsenic exposure
An eroded, nodular or bleeding area suggesting early invasion
Pigmented when on genital or perianal skin
dx.cf: Biopsy any persistent solitary scaly plaque that does not resolve; full-thickness epidermal atypia confirms squamous cell carcinoma in situ, and an eroded or nodular area suggests invasion.
dx.dsc: Clustered glomerular (coiled) vessels and small brown dots in a linear or patchy arrangement over a scaly surface - a useful separator from psoriasis and superficial BCC.
dx.hp: Full-thickness keratinocyte atypia with disordered maturation and mitoses at all levels (a windblown epidermis), with an intact basement membrane.
dx.assoc: Driven by sun exposure, HPV, prior arsenic and immunosuppression; a solitary persistent plaque warrants biopsy, and an invasive focus (nodularity, ulceration) mandates excision.
dx.mgmt: For in-situ disease - topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, cryotherapy, curettage, or photodynamic therapy; excision (Mohs for large or ill-defined lesions). Exclude invasion first.

dx.look: Sharply marginated erythematous scaly plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugging on the face, scalp and ears; lesions heal with atrophy, scarring and central hypopigmentation ringed by hyperpigmentation, and produce scarring alopecia on the scalp.
fr: Follicular plugging and adherent scale (a carpet-tack undersurface when peeled)
Photodistributed on the face, scalp and conchal bowl of the ear
Scarring, atrophy and dyspigmentation as lesions resolve
Scarring alopecia when on the scalp
More common and more disfiguring in skin of color
ag: Silvery lamellar scale in an extensor pattern
Greasy scale in the nasolabial folds
dx.cf: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (a granular lupus band) plus ANA; a minority progress to systemic lupus, so review systemic symptoms and serology.
dx.dsc: Follicular keratotic plugs, perifollicular whitish halos, thick arborizing vessels and pigment change within a scarred plaque.
dx.hp: Interface dermatitis with follicular plugging, a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, basement-membrane thickening and dermal mucin; direct immunofluorescence shows a lupus band.
dx.assoc: Check ANA and screen for systemic lupus (a minority progress); scarring is permanent, so treat early, and advise smoking cessation, which improves antimalarial efficacy.
dx.mgmt: Strict photoprotection, potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids, and hydroxychloroquine first-line; stop smoking.

dx.look: Sharply marginated, salmon-red plaques with adherent silvery-white lamellar scale. Symmetric on extensor elbows, knees, sacrum and scalp. Nail pitting, onycholysis and the pathognomonic oil-drop sign in about a quarter.
fr: Sharp, palpable margin — you can trace the edge with a fingernail
Extensor and sacral distribution, symmetric
Scalp involvement crossing the hairline onto forehead
Nail pits, oil-drop sign, distal onycholysis
Koebner phenomenon in scratch lines
Auspitz sign: punctate bleeding on scale removal
ag: Greasy yellow scale in nasolabial folds instead of silvery scale
Central clearing with an active advancing edge
Lesions confined to one region without symmetry
dx.cf: Diagnosis is clinical. Biopsy only when the picture is atypical or when distinguishing from mycosis fungoides or PRP changes management.
dx.dsc: Regularly distributed dotted (glomerular) vessels over a light-red background with diffuse white scale; the uniformity of the vessel pattern is the dermoscopic hallmark.
dx.hp: Confluent parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses, regular psoriasiform acanthosis with thinned suprapapillary plates, and dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae.
dx.assoc: Psoriatic arthritis in up to a third, plus metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and inflammatory bowel disease - ask about joint symptoms and screen cardiometabolic risk. Guttate flares follow streptococcal pharyngitis.
dx.mgmt: Localized disease - a topical vitamin D analog (calcipotriene) with a topical corticosteroid; extensive disease - narrowband UVB, then methotrexate, acitretin, cyclosporine, or a biologic.

dx.look: Ill-defined erythema with greasy yellow-orange scale in sebaceous areas: scalp, eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, retroauricular, presternal. Waxes and wanes. In infants, cradle cap and a sharply marginated exudative napkin eruption.
fr: Nasolabial folds, eyebrows, glabella, retroauricular
Greasy yellowish scale rather than dry silvery scale
Poorly defined margins
Presternal and interscapular patches
Improves in summer, flares in winter
ag: Sharply marginated plaques on extensor surfaces
dx.cf: Clinical. Consider HIV testing when severe, refractory, or unusually extensive — severe seborrheic dermatitis is an HIV marker.
dx.dsc: Patchy thin or arborizing vessels with greasy yellowish scale in a nonspecific pattern; the absence of the regular dotted vessels of psoriasis is the useful clue.
dx.hp: Superficial perivascular infiltrate with spongiosis and scale-crust (parakeratosis) at the edges of the follicular ostia (shoulder parakeratosis).
dx.assoc: Severe, refractory or explosive disease is an HIV marker - offer testing; also more common and more severe in Parkinson disease and other neurologic disorders.
dx.mgmt: Topical antifungal (ketoconazole) with a low-potency corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor; medicated shampoos (ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide) for the scalp.

dx.look: Annular or polycyclic plaque with a raised scaly advancing edge and central clearing. Asymmetric, often single or few. Look for concurrent tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis as the reservoir.
fr: Central clearing with an active, scaly, advancing border
Asymmetric or unilateral
Concurrent tinea pedis or onychomycosis
Recent topical steroid use with paradoxical spread (tinea incognito)
Animal contact, occlusion, humid climate
ag: Silvery lamellar scale without an advancing edge
Negative KOH from an adequately scraped active edge
dx.cf: KOH from the scaly advancing edge. Culture if KOH is negative but suspicion persists, or before committing to systemic therapy.
dx.dsc: Peripheral white scale on the advancing edge, with broken or bent (morse-code) hairs where vellus hair is involved; the background is otherwise nonspecific.
dx.hp: PAS-positive septate hyphae confined to the stratum corneum (the sandwich sign - fungus between two cornified layers) over a mildly spongiotic epidermis.
dx.assoc: Hunt for the reservoir - tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis - and for zoophilic contact; widespread or recalcitrant disease should prompt thought about immunosuppression.
dx.mgmt: Topical azole or allylamine (terbinafine) for localized disease; oral terbinafine or itraconazole when extensive, follicular (Majocchi granuloma), or steroid-modified.

dx.look: A herald patch in about 80%, followed 1–2 weeks later by oval salmon-colored papules and patches with a trailing collarette of scale, aligned along skin cleavage lines in a Christmas-tree pattern on the trunk. Self-limited over 6–12 weeks. HHV-6/7 reactivation.
fr: Herald patch preceding the eruption by 1–2 weeks
Fine collarette scale trailing the inner edge of each lesion
Long axes following cleavage lines, Christmas-tree pattern on the back
Spares face, palms and soles
Age 10–35, spring or autumn
ag: Palm and sole involvement — that is secondary syphilis until disproved
dx.cf: Clinical. Always send a treponemal test if palms, soles or mucosa are involved, or if there is any sexual risk history — secondary syphilis is the great mimic here.
dx.dsc: A peripheral collarette of scale over a nonspecific dotted-vessel background; dermoscopy mainly confirms the trailing scale.
dx.hp: Mounds of focal parakeratosis, mild spongiosis and extravasated erythrocytes in the papillary dermis - supportive rather than specific.
dx.assoc: HHV-6/7 reactivation; a pityriasis rosea-like drug eruption (ACE inhibitors and others) is the main mimic. Palm, sole or mucosal involvement should trigger syphilis serology.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance - it is self-limited over 6-12 weeks; treat itch with an emollient, topical corticosteroid or antihistamine. UVB or oral acyclovir may shorten severe early disease.

dx.look: The six Ps: purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules and plaques, with fine white Wickham striae on the surface. Flexor wrists, shins, lumbar. Oral reticulate white lacework in 40–60%. Koebnerizes. Heals with marked post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
fr: Violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules
Wickham striae — seen best under mineral oil with a hand lens
Flexural wrists, ankles, shins
Reticulate white buccal lacework
Intense pruritus
Nail: longitudinal ridging, pterygium
ag: Absent oral findings in widespread disease
dx.cf: Biopsy shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the epidermis with basal liquefaction and Civatte bodies. Screen for hepatitis C. Review the drug list — lichenoid drug eruption is clinically near-identical.
dx.dsc: White crossing (Wickham) striae over a violaceous background with peripheral dotted vessels - the striae are the diagnostic feature.
dx.hp: A band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermoepidermal junction, basal vacuolar degeneration, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, sawtooth rete ridges and Civatte bodies.
dx.assoc: Screen for hepatitis C, particularly in erosive or oral disease; review the drug list, since a lichenoid drug eruption is clinically near-identical.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical corticosteroids first-line (intralesional or oral for erosive, nail or widespread disease); topical calcineurin inhibitors for oral and genital lesions; phototherapy or acitretin when extensive.

dx.look: Coin-shaped, intensely pruritic plaques of coalescing vesicles and papules on a background of xerosis, most often on the extensor legs and dorsal hands of older adults in winter.
fr: Coin-shaped, sharply defined but not sharply scaled
Weeping or crusted rather than silvery
Marked pruritus
Background xerosis, winter onset, older adult
dx.cf: Clinical. KOH to exclude tinea, which it closely mimics. Patch test if the distribution suggests contact.
dx.dsc: Patchy dotted vessels with yellowish serocrust in a nonspecific eczematous pattern; dermoscopy is used mainly to help exclude tinea.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis with acanthosis and a serum-scale crust - indistinguishable from other eczemas; biopsy serves to exclude tinea or mycosis fungoides.
dx.assoc: Background xerosis and atopy; nickel or other contact allergy can drive persistent lesions - patch test refractory cases, and exclude tinea with KOH.
dx.mgmt: Liberal emollients with a mid- to high-potency topical corticosteroid; treat secondary staphylococcal infection and correct the underlying dry skin.

dx.look: Non-pruritic coppery-red papulosquamous eruption involving the palms and soles, with generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches, condylomata lata and a moth-eaten alopecia. Occurs weeks to months after the chancre.
fr: Palm and sole involvement
Coppery or ham-colored hue
Generalized lymphadenopathy, including epitrochlear
Absent or minimal pruritus
Moth-eaten patchy alopecia
Mucous patches or condylomata lata
dx.cf: Treponemal test plus RPR/VDRL titer. Dark-field or PCR of a moist lesion when available. Offer HIV testing to everyone diagnosed.
dx.hp: A psoriasiform and lichenoid dermatitis with a plasma-cell-rich infiltrate and endothelial swelling; spirochetes are shown on Warthin-Starry stain or immunohistochemistry.
dx.assoc: A marker of HIV risk - offer HIV testing to everyone diagnosed; screen for other sexually transmitted infections and notify partners.
dx.mgmt: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly for early syphilis; doxycycline if penicillin-allergic and not pregnant. Report to public health and trace contacts.

dx.n: Mycosis fungoides, patch or plaque stage
dx.look: Persistent, asymmetric, irregularly shaped scaly patches with a fine wrinkled or poikilodermatous surface, characteristically in the double-covered bathing-trunk distribution. Sun-protected sites. Present for years and repeatedly labeled as eczema or psoriasis.
fr: Persistent for years despite adequate topical steroid
Bathing-trunk or other sun-protected distribution
Irregular, bizarre, non-symmetric outlines
Poikiloderma: atrophy, telangiectasia, mottled pigment
Variable-sized patches of differing ages
ag: Recent onset in a young patient
dx.cf: Multiple biopsies from untreated sites, repeated over time if the first is non-diagnostic. Request T cell receptor gene rearrangement. Stop topical steroids for 2–4 weeks before biopsy or the histology will be flattened.
dx.dsc: Fine short linear or spermatozoa-like vessels with orange-yellow structureless areas; patchy and asymmetric in early disease.
dx.hp: Epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei, Pautrier microabscesses and lymphocytes lined up along the basal layer; often subtle in early disease.
dx.assoc: Send T-cell receptor gene rearrangement; stage with nodal exam and, when advanced, flow cytometry for Sezary cells. Stop topical steroids 2-4 weeks before biopsy.
dx.mgmt: Skin-directed therapy for early stage - topical corticosteroids, topical nitrogen mustard, bexarotene gel, or phototherapy (NB-UVB or PUVA); refer to a cutaneous-lymphoma service.

dx.look: Photodistributed annular-polycyclic or psoriasiform plaques on the upper back, shoulders, V of the neck and extensor arms. Spares the knuckles and the mid-face. Non-scarring, resolves with dyspigmentation. Anti-Ro/SSA positive in the majority.
fr: Strict photodistribution sparing sun-shadowed sites
Sparing of the knuckles
Annular-polycyclic with a fine peripheral scale
Drug trigger: hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPIs, TNF inhibitors
Non-scarring, heals with hypopigmentation
ag: Follicular plugging and scarring — that suggests discoid lupus
Silvery scale in an extensor pattern
dx.cf: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence from a lesion, plus ANA, anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB. Review the drug list carefully.
dx.hp: Interface (vacuolar) dermatitis with basal damage, dermal mucin and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows a granular lupus band.
dx.assoc: Anti-Ro/SSA positive in the majority - check ANA, anti-Ro and anti-La; review drugs (hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPIs, TNF inhibitors) and assess for systemic lupus.
dx.mgmt: Strict photoprotection, a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor, and hydroxychloroquine first-line; stop any culprit drug.

dx.look: Reddish-orange follicular hyperkeratotic papules coalescing into psoriasiform plaques spreading cephalocaudally, with sharply demarcated islands of normal skin and a waxy orange palmoplantar keratoderma.
fr: Islands of sparing within confluent erythema
Salmon-orange rather than salmon-pink hue
Follicular plugging on the dorsal proximal phalanges (nutmeg-grater feel)
Waxy orange keratoderma of palms and soles
Cephalocaudal progression
ag: Silvery scale with clean margins and no follicular accentuation
dx.cf: Biopsy is suggestive rather than diagnostic: alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in a checkerboard, broad short rete ridges.
dx.dsc: Follicular keratotic plugs surrounded by erythema with islands of spared skin; vessels are nonspecific.
dx.hp: Alternating ortho- and parakeratosis in a checkerboard pattern, follicular plugging, and broad short rete ridges.
dx.assoc: Usually idiopathic; type 6 is HIV-associated - test when atypical or refractory. Cephalocaudal spread may progress to erythroderma, so watch thermoregulation.
dx.mgmt: Emollients and keratolytics with a corticosteroid for limited disease; a systemic retinoid (acitretin or isotretinoin) or methotrexate first-line for extensive disease.

dx.look: Widespread violaceous to dusky scaly papules and plaques that look like lichen planus or psoriasis but are more extensive, more scaly and often photodistributed. Begins weeks to months after the drug is started, not days. Wickham striae are sparse or absent and the mouth is usually spared.
fr: New drug started weeks to months before the eruption
More widespread and more scaly than idiopathic lichen planus
Photodistributed accentuation on the forearms, V of the neck and shins
Wickham striae poorly formed or absent, oral lesions uncommon
Thiazide, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor, antimalarial, gold, allopurinol or a checkpoint inhibitor
Clears slowly after withdrawal, over 1 to 4 months
ag: No new drug in the preceding 6 months
Dense reticulate buccal lacework with flexor wrist papules
Sharply marginated silvery extensor plaques with nail pits
dx.cf: Read the medication list against the date of onset. Biopsy shows a lichenoid infiltrate with features atypical for lichen planus: eosinophils, plasma cells, focal parakeratosis and a deeper perivascular infiltrate. The definitive test is clearance after withdrawal, which takes 1 to 4 months.
dx.dsc: Violaceous background with sparse, poorly formed white striae, unlike the well-organized crossing Wickham striae of idiopathic lichen planus.
dx.hp: A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate with basal vacuolar change plus focal parakeratosis, eosinophils and plasma cells, and a deeper perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate than is seen in lichen planus.
dx.assoc: Culprits include thiazides, beta blockers, ACE inhibitors (captopril), antimalarials, gold, penicillamine, calcium channel blockers, carbamazepine, lithium, allopurinol and anti-PD-1 agents. Extensive disease can progress to exfoliative dermatitis, and adnexal involvement causes alopecia and anhidrosis.
dx.mgmt: Stop the culprit drug - the eruption clears over 1 to 4 months, and up to 24 months after gold. Potent topical corticosteroids and photoprotection meanwhile; phototherapy or acitretin for refractory extensive disease.

dx.look: Successive crops of small reddish-brown scaling papules, each capped by a single mica-like scale that lifts off intact when gently scraped. Trunk and proximal limbs of an adolescent or young adult, mostly asymptomatic, resolving with hypo- and hyperpigmentation.
fr: Crops of lesions of clearly different ages present at the same time
A single adherent mica-like scale detached in one piece by gentle scraping
Reddish-brown papules on the trunk and proximal extremities
Adolescent or young adult, more often male
Postinflammatory hypo- and hyperpigmentation as lesions resolve
ag: Silvery lamellar scale with a sharp palpable edge
Hemorrhagic crusting and varioliform scarring, which is PLEVA
dx.cf: Clinical, confirmed by biopsy of a fresh untreated papule. If lesions are necrotic and hemorrhagically crusted the diagnosis is PLEVA, and lymphomatoid papulosis must be excluded histologically because it is clinically almost indistinguishable.
dx.dsc: Focal orange-yellow structureless areas with a central adherent white scale and fine peripheral dotted or linear vessels.
dx.hp: Parakeratosis with mild spongiosis, scattered necrotic keratinocytes, lymphocytic exocytosis and extravasated erythrocytes in the papillary dermis. PLEVA adds epidermal necrosis and a wedge-shaped infiltrate reaching the deep reticular dermis.
dx.assoc: Regarded as a T cell response to an infectious trigger. The clinically important association is lymphomatoid papulosis, which mimics PLEVA - request CD30 staining when lesions are necrotic, and follow up rather than treating blindly.
dx.mgmt: Many need no treatment. Oral erythromycin or a tetracycline for a 2 to 4 week trial first-line; natural sunlight, narrowband UVB or PUVA when antibiotics fail. Resolves over 6 to 12 months and may relapse years later.

dx.look: Psoriasiform scaling plaques on the scalp, elbows and buttocks with brown-red papules and pustules that crust into thick hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles - keratoderma blennorrhagicum. Usually a young man with an asymmetric oligoarthritis 1 to 4 weeks after urethritis or dysentery. Circinate balanitis gives shallow erosions with a serpiginous micropustular border on the glans.
fr: Asymmetric oligoarthritis of knees, ankles and small joints of the feet
Crusted hyperkeratotic papules and pustules on palms and soles
Circinate balanitis with a serpiginous micropustular border
Urethritis, cervicitis or dysentery 1 to 4 weeks before onset
Conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis
Young man, often HLA-B27 positive
ag: No joint, eye or genitourinary symptoms at all
Older woman with no preceding infection
Long-standing symmetric extensor plaques with a strong family history of psoriasis
dx.cf: Clinical. Only 30% have the full triad of arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis and 40% have a single manifestation, so any one of them with psoriasiform acral lesions is enough to pursue. Urethral culture and chlamydia NAAT, stool culture, HLA-B27, ESR and CRP; exclude disseminated gonococcal infection.
dx.hp: Early spongiosis and vesiculation, later psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with spongiform pustules and parakeratosis over a superficial perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate and dermal edema - essentially indistinguishable from pustular psoriasis.
dx.assoc: Triggered by Chlamydia or Ureaplasma urethritis, or Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia or Campylobacter enteritis. HLA-B27 in up to 75% of White patients; incidence is increased in HIV infection, so test. Most resolve in 3 to 12 months, but 10 to 20% develop chronic deforming arthritis.
dx.mgmt: Treat the skin as psoriasis: potent topical corticosteroids under occlusion for palms and soles, low-potency for balanitis, and acitretin, phototherapy or a TNF inhibitor when extensive. NSAIDs and rest for the joints with rheumatology referral; treat documented chlamydial infection and the partner.

dx.look: Generalized dry skin with fine powdery to large, tessellated, tightly bound-down fish-scale scaling, worst on the shins and worse in winter. The antecubital and popliteal fossae and axillae are spared, the palms and soles are hyperlinear, and keratosis pilaris roughens the outer upper arms and thighs.
fr: Scale is bound down and tessellated, heaviest on the shins
Antecubital and popliteal fossae and axillae spared
Hyperlinear palms and soles
Keratosis pilaris on the outer upper arms and thighs
Lifelong, starting in the first year, better in summer and humid climates
Personal or family history of atopy
dx.cf: Clinical - bound-down scale sparing the flexures, hyperlinear palms and keratosis pilaris together are diagnostic. Abrupt onset in an adult is acquired ichthyosis instead, and demands a search for lymphoma, HIV, thyroid disease, malnutrition and drugs.
dx.hp: Compact hyperkeratosis with a reduced or absent granular layer, small poorly formed keratohyalin granules and a flattened germinative layer.
dx.assoc: Autosomal dominant, filaggrin-deficient, and common at roughly 1 in 250. Over half also have atopic dermatitis. New scaling in an adult is acquired ichthyosis until proven otherwise and is a recognized marker of lymphoma and HIV disease.
dx.mgmt: Hydrate then occlude: bathe and apply petrolatum immediately, with urea-containing or alpha-hydroxy acid (lactic or glycolic) creams as keratolytics. Systemic retinoids only for severe disease, with monitoring.

dx.look: Sharply marginated tan to pink-brown patches with fine wrinkled scale in the groin, axillae, inframammary folds or toe webs, essentially asymptomatic and with no advancing edge. Coral-red fluorescence under a Wood lamp settles it at the bedside.
fr: Confined to intertriginous skin - groin, axillae, inframammary folds, toe webs
Sharply marginated tan or brown patch with fine scale and little inflammation
Asymptomatic or only mildly itchy
Coral-red fluorescence under a Wood lamp
Obesity, diabetes, hyperhidrosis, occlusion or a humid climate
ag: Raised scaly advancing edge with central clearing
dx.cf: Wood lamp shows coral-red fluorescence from porphyrins produced by Corynebacterium minutissimum. KOH is negative, which excludes dermatophytosis - although the two coexist in the toe webs often enough that finding one does not end the search.
dx.hp: Rarely needed: filamentous and coccoid organisms in the stratum corneum on Gram or PAS stain over a normal or mildly acanthotic epidermis.
dx.assoc: Overgrowth of Corynebacterium minutissimum favored by a humid, occluded microclimate. Look for obesity, diabetes and hyperhidrosis, and expect recurrence unless the microclimate changes.
dx.mgmt: Benzoyl peroxide wash or an alcohol sanitizing gel with topical clindamycin or erythromycin; oral erythromycin for extensive disease. Keep the fold dry, treat hyperhidrosis, and treat coexisting tinea.

dx.look: Dry, superficially fissured skin in a cracked-porcelain or dried-riverbed pattern of fine red fissures, typically over the shins of an older adult in winter, itchy out of proportion to what is visible. Repeated hot soapy bathing and heated, dry indoor air are the drivers.
fr: Shins of an older adult in winter, in a heated, low-humidity home
Cracked-porcelain or dried-riverbed pattern of superficial red fissures
Background xerosis with fine scaling
Itch out of proportion to the visible change
Frequent hot soapy baths or showers
ag: Sharply marginated plaques with silvery lamellar scale
Active scaly advancing edge with central clearing
Onset in a young adult in summer
dx.cf: Clinical. If it does not settle with emollients and a mid-potency corticosteroid, reconsider: intractable eczema in this age group can be pre-bullous pemphigoid, and a fixed asymmetric patch can be early mycosis fungoides.
dx.hp: Mild spongiosis with hyperkeratosis, a compact stratum corneum and a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate - nonspecific, and used only to exclude other diagnoses.
dx.assoc: Driven by low ambient humidity, overbathing and age-related barrier loss. Consider hypothyroidism, malnutrition, and drugs (diuretics, statins, retinoids); persistent itch with urticarial plaques should prompt a perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence.
dx.mgmt: Stop soap and hot tub baths, raise indoor humidity above 50%, and apply an ointment emollient immediately after tepid bathing. A mid-potency corticosteroid ointment twice daily until the inflammation settles, then emollient alone through the winter.
dx.pat: Shins of older adults in winter

ctx.s: Guttate psoriasis follows streptococcal infection, Fitzpatrick 8e §3

ctx.l: New drug in the last 8 weeks
ctx.s: Drug-induced SCLE and lichenoid eruptions, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

ctx.l: Sexual risk exposure in the last 6 months
ctx.s: Pre-test probability of syphilis rises sharply with exposure history
Severe seborrheic dermatitis and explosive psoriasis are HIV markers, Fitzpatrick 8e §2,§3

ctx.l: Treated with a topical steroid and got worse
Present for more than 2 years, never fully clears
ctx.s: Chronicity is the single most useful discriminator for MF

ctx.l: Dry heated indoor climate, or daily hot soapy bathing
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - asteatotic dermatitis follows low humidity and overbathing

ctx.l: Enteric or genitourinary infection in the last 6 weeks
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - reactive arthritis begins 1 to 4 weeks after enteric or genitourinary infection

find.l: Sharply marginated plaque with silvery lamellar scale
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Auspitz sign — punctate bleeding after scale removal
find.s: Suggestive of psoriasis but not specific, Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction

find.l: Nail pitting, oil-drop sign or distal onycholysis
find.s: Nail changes in about 25% of psoriasis; oil-drop sign is pathognomonic, Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Greasy yellow scale in nasolabial folds and eyebrows
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2

find.l: Central clearing with a raised, scaly, advancing edge
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §26

find.l: Asymmetric or unilateral distribution
find.s: Symmetry is a core feature of the endogenous papulosquamous disorders

find.l: Concurrent tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis
find.s: Autoinoculation from a reservoir site, Fitzpatrick 8e §26

find.l: Herald patch preceded the eruption
find.s: Herald patch in ~80% of pityriasis rosea, Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Collarette of scale trailing the inner edge of lesions
find.s: Marginal collarette distinguishes pityriasis rosea from guttate psoriasis, Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Long axes follow skin cleavage lines (Christmas tree)
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Wickham striae on the lesion surface
find.s: Best seen with a hand lens after mineral oil, Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction

find.l: Reticulate white lacework on buccal mucosa
find.s: Oral involvement in 40–60% of lichen planus, Fitzpatrick 8e §33

find.l: Palms and soles involved
find.s: Palmoplantar involvement is the classic discriminator for secondary syphilis, Fitzpatrick 8e §30

find.l: Generalized lymphadenopathy
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §30, §21

find.l: Little or no pruritus
find.s: Secondary syphilis is characteristically non-pruritic; lichen planus and nummular eczema are intensely itchy

find.l: Strictly photodistributed, sparing sun-shadowed sites
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Islands of normal skin within confluent erythema
find.s: Sharply demarcated islands of sparing are near-specific for PRP, Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Follicular hyperkeratotic papules, nutmeg-grater feel
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3

find.l: Poikiloderma: atrophy, telangiectasia, mottled pigment
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §21

find.l: Bathing-trunk or other sun-protected distribution
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §21

find.l: Coin-shaped weeping or crusted plaques with xerosis
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2

find.l: Koebner phenomenon in scratch or scar lines
find.s: Koebnerization occurs in psoriasis and lichen planus, Fitzpatrick 8e §3,§14

find.l: A solitary fixed plaque that persists or grows despite adequate treatment
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin

find.l: Follicular plugging with scarring, atrophy and dyspigmentation
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin

find.l: Widespread scaly violaceous eruption in a photoexposed distribution
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23 Table 23-4 - lichenoid drug eruptions are more extensive and more scaly than lichen planus

find.l: Eruption only began to clear after a drug was stopped, over 1 to 4 months
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23 Table 23-4 - resolution after withdrawal is slow, 1 to 4 months

find.l: Crops of papules of clearly different ages appearing over weeks
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3 - new lesions appear in successive crops

find.l: A single mica-like scale lifted off intact by gentle scraping
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3 - central mica-like scale of pityriasis lichenoides chronica

find.l: Crusted hyperkeratotic papules and pustules on palms and soles
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - keratoderma blennorrhagicum

find.l: Asymmetric oligoarthritis with urethritis or conjunctivitis
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Circinate balanitis with a serpiginous micropustular border
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Bound-down fish-scale scaling on the shins with spared antecubital and popliteal fossae
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §4

find.l: Hyperlinear palms with keratosis pilaris of the outer arms
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §4

find.l: Confined to skin folds - groin, axillae, inframammary or toe webs
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - erythrasma is confined to intertriginous skin

find.l: Sharply marginated tan-brown patch with fine wrinkled scale and no advancing edge
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25

find.l: Cracked-porcelain fissuring over dry skin of the shins
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - eczema craquele

find.l: Flares every winter and clears in summer
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2,§4 - xerotic dermatoses worsen with low winter humidity

find.l: Peeled scale shows carpet-tack keratotic spines on its undersurface
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - follicular plugging of chronic cutaneous lupus

find.l: Clustered glomerular (coiled) vessels on dermoscopy of a solitary scaly plaque
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - glomerular vessels separate Bowen disease from psoriasis and superficial BCC

test.l: Punch or shave biopsy for histopathology
test.w: Any solitary scaly plaque that persists or enlarges despite adequate topical therapy, especially on sun-damaged or lower-leg skin.
test.p: Full-thickness keratinocyte atypia confirms squamous cell carcinoma in situ. Treat, and look for any invasive focus.
test.n: A benign biopsy of a clinically suspicious plaque may reflect sampling - re-biopsy the thickest or most atypical area if suspicion persists.
test.x: Sample an untreated, representative area; a superficial shave can miss early invasion at the base.

test.l: KOH preparation from the scaly advancing edge
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §26 — positive in ~90% when adequately sampled and untreated
test.w: Do it on every scaly plaque before you reach for a topical steroid. It costs three minutes and it is the single most cost-effective test in general dermatology.
test.p: Septate branching hyphae confirm dermatophytosis. Treat, and look for the reservoir — feet, groin, nails.
test.n: A negative does not exclude tinea if the patient has been using a topical steroid or an antifungal. If the picture still fits, culture or repeat after two weeks off treatment.
test.x: Sample the active edge, not the cleared center. Scrape firmly. A tongue-tip-equivalent sample is why negatives are falsely reassuring. Chlorazol black E or Swartz-Lamkin stain improves yield.

test.w: When KOH is negative but suspicion persists, when species identification matters (tinea capitis, animal contact), or before committing to systemic terbinafine.
test.p: Confirms and speciates. Zoophilic species should prompt a look at the household animal.
test.n: Does not exclude if the patient was pretreated. Two to four weeks for a result is a real clinical cost.
test.x: Slow. Do not withhold treatment on a strong clinical picture while waiting.

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3 — histology is characteristic but not pathognomonic
test.w: When the clinical picture is atypical, when the diagnosis changes systemic therapy, or when mycosis fungoides is in the differential.
test.p: Confluent parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, thinning over elongated papillae, regular acanthosis. Supports psoriasis.
test.n: Non-diagnostic histology in a clinically convincing case does not overturn the clinical diagnosis — it usually means the lesion was treated or sampled at the wrong stage.
test.x: Choose an untreated lesion. Two weeks off topical steroid before biopsy substantially improves the yield.

test.l: Multiple biopsies with T cell receptor gene rearrangement
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §21 — early MF is notoriously difficult to confirm histologically
test.w: Any scaly eruption persisting for years in a sun-protected distribution that has never fully cleared on adequate topical therapy.
test.p: Epidermotropism, Pautrier microabscesses and a clonal rearrangement together support MF. Stage and refer.
test.n: A single negative biopsy does not exclude early MF. Serial biopsies over months are often required and that is normal, not a failure.
test.x: Topical steroids suppress the infiltrate. Stop them for 2–4 weeks first. Sample the thickest, most infiltrated, least treated patch.

test.l: Treponemal test (TPPA/EIA) with RPR or VDRL titer
test.w: Any papulosquamous eruption involving palms or soles, any non-pruritic generalized eruption with lymphadenopathy, and anyone with a sexual risk history. The threshold to test should be very low.
test.p: Confirms syphilis. Stage it, treat with benzathine penicillin G, notify partners, and offer HIV testing.
test.n: A negative treponemal test effectively excludes secondary syphilis — secondary disease is a serologically florid stage.
test.x: The prozone phenomenon can give a falsely negative or low RPR in very high-titer disease. Ask the lab to dilute if the clinical picture is strong.

test.l: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence, plus ANA and anti-Ro/SSA
test.w: Photodistributed annular or psoriasiform plaques, especially with a new drug in the preceding weeks to months.
test.p: Interface dermatitis with a positive lupus band, plus anti-Ro/SSA, confirms SCLE. Screen for systemic involvement and review the drug list.
test.n: Anti-Ro is negative in a minority of genuine SCLE. Weigh the histology and the photodistribution above the serology.
test.x: Drug-induced SCLE is serologically and histologically identical to idiopathic. The only way to find it is to read the medication list. Hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPIs and TNF inhibitors are the usual culprits.

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2,§3 — severe seborrheic dermatitis and explosive psoriasis are recognized HIV markers
test.w: Severe, extensive or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis; sudden explosive psoriasis; any syphilis diagnosis; PRP type 6.
test.p: Changes the whole management frame. Refer for antiretroviral therapy — the dermatosis often improves with it.
test.n: Excludes HIV as the driver. Look elsewhere for the cause of severity.
test.x: Test in the window period gives a false negative. Repeat at 6 weeks if the exposure was recent.

test.l: Wood lamp examination of the affected fold
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 and Introduction - coral-red fluorescence; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Any sharply marginated brown or pink patch in the groin, axilla, inframammary fold or toe web, before treating it as tinea or inverse psoriasis.
test.p: Coral-red fluorescence confirms erythrasma. Treat with a benzoyl peroxide wash plus topical clindamycin or erythromycin, and change the microclimate or it returns.
test.n: A negative does not exclude it if the area was washed recently - bathing removes the porphyrin that fluoresces. Re-examine before the next wash and send a KOH.
test.x: Examine in a fully darkened room, and remember that erythrasma and interdigital tinea pedis frequently coexist. Finding one does not stop the search for the other.

test.l: Punch biopsy of a fresh untreated papule, with CD30 if necrotic
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §3 - clinical diagnosis confirmed by skin biopsy; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Crops of scaly papules of differing ages in an adolescent or young adult, and promptly when lesions are necrotic or hemorrhagically crusted.
test.p: Parakeratosis, necrotic keratinocytes, lymphocytic exocytosis and extravasated erythrocytes support pityriasis lichenoides. Treat with erythromycin or a tetracycline, or phototherapy.
test.n: Nonspecific histology does not exclude it. Sample a fresh untreated papule and weigh the crops of differing ages more heavily than the slide.
test.x: If large atypical CD30-positive cells are present this is lymphomatoid papulosis, not PLEVA. That distinction changes follow-up entirely, so ask for CD30 whenever the lesions are necrotic.

test.l: Dated medication timeline with planned drug withdrawal
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23 Table 23-4 - resolution after withdrawal takes 1 to 4 months; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Any lichenoid or psoriasiform eruption that is unusually extensive, photodistributed, or started weeks to months after a new drug.
test.p: Clearance after withdrawal confirms it. Record the drug as a documented reaction so that it is never restarted.
test.n: No improvement at 4 weeks does not exclude a drug cause - these eruptions resolve over 1 to 4 months, and up to 24 months after gold.
test.x: Rechallenge is not needed and is not safe practice. Build the timeline against every drug started in the preceding 6 months, including over-the-counter NSAIDs and supplements.

test.l: HLA-B27, inflammatory markers, and enteric and genitourinary cultures
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - HLA-B27 in up to 75% of White patients with reactive arthritis; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Psoriasiform acral plaques or circinate balanitis with arthritis, urethritis, dysentery or conjunctivitis.
test.p: Supports reactive arthritis. Treat the skin as psoriasis, refer to rheumatology, treat a documented chlamydial infection and the partner, and offer HIV testing.
test.n: HLA-B27 negative disease occurs and runs a milder course with less sacroiliitis and uveitis. A negative result does not overturn the clinical diagnosis.
test.x: Urethral culture must be negative for gonococcus before you settle on this. Disseminated gonococcal infection also produces acral pustules with arthritis, and it needs antibiotics rather than topical steroids.

test.l: Biopsy for the granular layer, plus an acquired-ichthyosis screen if onset is in adulthood
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §4 - reduced or absent granular layer; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Rarely needed in a lifelong case. Do it when generalized bound-down scaling appears for the first time in an adult.
test.p: Compact hyperkeratosis with a reduced or absent granular layer supports ichthyosis vulgaris. In adult-onset disease go on to screen for lymphoma, HIV, thyroid disease, malnutrition and drugs.
test.n: A normal granular layer argues against ichthyosis vulgaris. X-linked ichthyosis keeps its granular layer, has dirty brown scale, involves the flexures and spares the palms and soles.
test.x: Do not biopsy an obvious lifelong case. The entire value of this test is catching acquired ichthyosis, which is a marker of internal disease.

test.l: Two-week trial of soap avoidance, ointment emollient and a mid-potency corticosteroid
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Fissured, dry, itchy shins in an older adult in winter, where the diagnosis is clinical and the question is whether anything else is going on.
test.p: Clearance confirms asteatotic dermatitis. Keep the emollient going through the winter - recurrence is the rule if bathing habits and indoor humidity do not change.
test.n: Failure to clear calls for a rethink, not a stronger steroid. Intractable eczema in this age group can be pre-bullous pemphigoid - look for urticarial plaques and send perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence.
test.x: Creams sting fissured skin and work less well than ointments. Prescribing a potent steroid without addressing bathing and humidity is the usual reason this fails.

flag: Every scaly plaque deserves a KOH before it receives a topical steroid. The two costliest errors in this presentation are tinea incognito, created by steroid applied to undiagnosed dermatophytosis, and mycosis fungoides mislabeled as eczema for a decade.
